38: The Home Rule Leagues (1916-18) and NCM (1920-22) taught urban workers and rural ryots to take part in politics.
Big landlords (zamindars and taluqdars) levied illegal abwabs and nazrana, evicted at will (bedakhli), and forced hari and begar.
The UP Kisan Sabha was set up in Feb 1918 by Mishra and Dwivedi with Malaviya as senior patron.
In 1921 the British used the Seditious Meetings Act (1911) to crush the agitation.
The Eka Movement had the same grievances plus thikedars (rent collectors) and the same methods. Madari Pasi, from the lower castes, led it.
Muslim tenants, the Mapillas, were part of Khilafat and angry with Hindu Jenmies over rents and eviction. INC joined at first, but arrests of INC leaders left the revolt without guidance.
After NCM was withdrawn in 1922, Patel led Borsad against dacoits, police collusion and an additional police tax.
Bardoli had Kaliparaj and Ujaliparaj, the Hali system and a 30% revenue rise based on a miscalculation.
Udasi Mahants, enriched by Ranjit Singh RS01-39's land grants, controlled Gurudwaras and backed the British.
The British passed the Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925, and the elected SGPC took all Gurudwaras. Gandhi had already withdrawn support over the Nabha issue.
39: In World War I the Defence of India Act 1915 was used to jail many revolutionaries. The 1920 amnesty let them out. They joined Gandhiji's NCM 1920-22 with enthusiasm, leaving arms behind.
In February 1922 NCM was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura. The revolutionaries were deeply disappointed.
The Russian Revolution of 1917 spread communist thought. They now wanted to end class oppression as well as colonial oppression.
Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Jogesh Chatterjee, Chandrashekhar Azad and Sachin Sanyal founded HRA in 1924.
HRA looted cash from a train in the Kakori Robbery case, 1925. Many were arrested. Bismil and Ashfaqullah were hanged. Azad escaped. With its leaders gone, HRA went inactive.
Azad and Bhagat Singh revived HRA as HSRA 1928, adding 'Socialist'. Lala Lajpat Rai died of lathi injuries in November 1928.
The CLA was discussing the Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill, aimed at the working class and communists. Bhagat Singh and B.K.
Bengal revolutionaries backed Swarajist leader C.R. Das, so the British repressed Swarajists too. After Das died in 1925, Bengal Congress split between S.C. Bose (Yugantar) and J.M.
During CDM 1930-34, Surya Sen, a school teacher, set up the IRA and raided the Chittagong Armory.
Azad died at Alfred Park on 27 February 1931. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on 23 March 1931. The Chittagong group was crushed by 1933 and Surya Sen was hanged in 1934.
40: The Montague Statement of 1917 promised gradual Swaraj, and GOI Act 1919 was the first step with a review after 10 years.
All seven were British MPs under Sir John Simon, and Clement Attlee was one of them. Swaraj includes a say for Indians in their own constitution.
The Secretary of State for India, Birkenhead, challenged Indians in the British Parliament to draft a constitution themselves.
INC rejected the Commission and decided on an APC to draft the Principles of a Constitution. When Simon came again in October 1928, protests swept the country.

In December 1927 ML1906 sent Four Delhi Proposals to Motilal Nehru: three new Muslim Majority Provinces, one-third at the Centre, reservation in Punjab and Bengal, and joint electorates if all that wa
The APC under M.A. Ansari formed a Motilal Nehru committee in May 1928, and the Report came in August 1928.
Jinnah proposed Three Amendments in the APC: one-third at the Centre, Punjab-Bengal reservation until UAF, and residuary powers to Provinces. All were rejected. INC then approved the Nehru Report.
In March 1929 Jinnah issued the 14 Points, a summary of every communal demand ever made by any Muslim organisation. It became the blueprint of all later ML1906 politics.
The Butler Committee, appointed in 1927, reported in 1929 that Paramountcy over the States was re-affirmed and that States should not be moved into a Union of India without their consent.
On 31 October 1929 Irwin said Dominion Status is implicit in the Montague Statement and that the intent is to give it at a future date, with a Round Table Conference in London.
In November 1929 INC leaders set three conditions for joining the RTC.
41: The Manifesto asked for an RTC acting as a Constituent Assembly with dominion status, an INC majority among Indian delegates and amnesty in the Bomb in CLA and Meerut cases.
At Lahore (Dec 1929, Nehru presiding) INC made complete independence its goal, fixed 26 January 1930 as the pledge day, rejected the RTC, quit the legislatures and empowered the AICC to launch CDM.
Muslim leaders of INC wanted an INC-ML pact like Lucknow, capitalists feared the Great Depression, ML1906 spoke of Hindu raj, other parties envied INC's popularity and CPI1925 called INC bourgeois.
In January 1930 MG listed four middle-class, two peasant and five general demands, from the 1s 4d rupee to abolition of the salt tax. If the British met them, INC would not need to fight.
Salt was used by everyone, was neither a Hindu nor a bourgeois issue and carried little risk of immediate repression.
Rajaji marched to Vedaranniyam, Kelappan to Poyannur, Inchudi became the Second Dandi, Ankola the Bardoli of Karnataka, and Andhra built Sibirams. INC's organisation since 1920 made this possible.
Ghaffar Khan's Red Shirts met machine guns at Qissa Khwani Bazaar on 23 April 1930. The Royal Garhwal Rifles refused to fire on the unarmed Muslim crowd.
MG warned the British about the Dharasana raid and was arrested in May 1930. Naidu, Manilal and Imam Saheb led 2,500 volunteers against 400 police; Webb Miller's report shocked the world.

The Delhi Pact of 5 March 1931 suspended CDM and brought INC to the 2nd RTC. Bhagat Singh was hanged on 23 March, and Karachi approved the Pact amid black flags, with rights and an economic programme.
The 2nd RTC failed on separate electorates and MG resumed CDM. INC was banned in January 1932 and the Communal Award of August 1932 extended separate electorates to the Depressed Classes.
The Poona Pact (24 Sept 1932) replaced separate electorates with reserved seats raised from 71 to 147. MG's 2nd phase turned to anti-untouchability, with the Harijan Sevak Sangh, Fund and magazine.
42: Linlithgow36-43 implemented the Act in 1937 and admitted it was the best way to maintain control over India. It runs to 321 sections. Nothing in it was a gift of self-government.
Revolutionaries (HRA1924, HSRA1928, Chittagong Armory Raid 1930-33), the masses (Anti-Simon 1928, Civil Disobedience 1930-34) and the Great Depression of 1929 kept Britain nervous.
The Simon Commission (1927, no Indian member) reported in June 1930: provincial autonomy, nothing at the Centre, more franchise, separate electorates, Burma out.
The Act has two halves. The Centre half proposed a Federation of British India and Princely States with dyarchy at the Centre. The provincial half proposed autonomy with a still-powerful Governor.
The Federation needed at least 50% of Princes to sign the Instrument of Accession (Section 6). They feared two bosses, losing financial autonomy, low representation and democracy.
The Act of 1919 kept governing the Centre. The Federal Court was set up in 1937, but the Federal Assembly, Council of States and dyarchy at the Centre never began.
Dyarchy ended and all provincial subjects became transferred. A Premier and Council of Ministers became responsible to the Assembly.
Forty percent of the provincial Budget was non-votable.
Hold the Centre, hand over provinces and keep INC busy governing. Provincial leaders would become autonomous power centres, so Divide and Rule would be applied to INC itself.
INC contested for the same reason as the Pro-Changers of 1923: occupy the space and do Constructive Work, now with executive power. It won a majority in 6 provinces and formed ministries in 8 of 11.
Morale of cadre, peasants and workers rose, INC gained governance experience, and Praja Mandals or State People's Congresses spread in Princely States.
43: Teacher opens the chapter with one question: why did India become independent? The INM was the strong hero.
The British, the INC and the ML1906 bargain over four things: transfer of executive power (ToP), the kind of Swaraj, who drafts the Constitution (COI), and Unity (565 Princely States, Pakistan).
Britain declared war on Germany and declared India a belligerent. Viceroy Linlithgow36-43 did not consult a single Indian leader. This act of colonial arrogance set the tone for six years.
MG: unconditional support, because Britain was the victim of Axis aggression. Bose: Britain's weakness is India's chance, start a Civil Disobedience Movement now.
The INC asked for responsible government at the Centre, a post-war Constituent Assembly and a declaration of war aims. In return it would help the war effort.
The CWC refused to support the war and directed the Congress ministries to resign, ending the 28-month rule. Linlithgow36-43 panicked and promised Dominion Status after the war.
Advisory War Council, a bigger VEC, a post-war Constituent Assembly of mainly Indians, Dominion Status after the war, and no constitution without the consent of minorities.
The INC rejected Dominion Status and the backdoor partition in the veto. The ML feared a Hindu-majority Centre would ignore its veto, leaving it with neither power nor Pakistan.
In 1941 the VEC was expanded to 8 Indians out of 12, but Defence, Home and Finance stayed out of Indian hands.
Japan took Rangoon in March 1942. Under US and USSR pressure, Churchill sent Sir Stafford Cripps.
44: The Cripps Mission (1942) offered only vague post-war promises and nothing on real transfer of power during the war. It showed that Britain meant to rule on its own terms whatever Indians thought.
War inflation squeezed ordinary people while British policy ignored the rising cost of living.
The INC did not want Indians to meet a Japanese invasion in low morale and passive helplessness. MG's idea: a high-spirited, nationalist people would resist far better than a demoralised one.
The CWC accepted the idea at Wardha in July 1942. On 8 August 1942 the INC held a special session in Bombay and passed the QIM resolution demanding immediate Purna Swaraj.
The entire top INC leadership was arrested. The detailed resolution could not be made public, so the public knew only what MG said in the speech.
The mass struggle was not non-violent: crowds pulled up railway tracks, blew up bridges, cut telegraph wires and attacked stations, police stations, courts and post offices.
Under the Revolutionary Movement Ordinance and Defence of India Rules the press was gagged, aircraft carried machine guns, villages were fined and burnt, and 60,000 were arrested by the en
The Congress Socialist Party leaders ran an underground network: Achyut Patwardhan, Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali, JP and others.
Held at Aga Khan Palace, Pune, Gandhi refused to condemn the movement's violence and began a 21-day fast (1943) against British violence.
Ballia (Aug 1942, Chittu Pandey) was the first. Jatiya Sarkar at Midnapore (Dec 1942 to Sep 1944) had courts, school grants, rice, cyclone relief and the Vidyut Vahini.
Gandhi was released in May 1944 on health grounds and turned to constructive work. In June 1945 all INC leaders were freed for the Simla Conference, which formally ended QIM.
45: In 1943 roughly 5 million Indians died in Bengal although crops had not failed.
The Famine Inquiry Commission (1945) under Sir John Woodhead blamed natural factors and supply disruption and let the administration off.
Japan took Malaya in January 1942, Singapore in February and Burma in March. Territories held for decades fell in weeks, and thousands of Indian soldiers were now Prisoners of War.
After Singapore fell, Mohan Singh persuaded the Japanese to hand over Indian PoWs; 40,000 in Singapore joined and the First Division was formed in September 1942.
Bose broke with the Gandhian leadership, formed the Forward Bloc (May 1939) and left the Congress after Tripuri.
He crossed the Indian Ocean from a German to a Japanese submarine and reached Singapore in July 1943, where he took over the IIL and the INA from Rash Behari Bose.
On 21 October 1943 Netaji set up the Provisional Government of Free India with INA headquarters in Rangoon and Singapore.
In 1944 the INA and Japan attacked towards Kohima and Imphal and failed; INA soldiers were even short-changed on weapons and supplies.
In November 1945 Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sehgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were tried at the Red Fort.
In February 1946 ratings on HMIS Talwar struck over fear of unemployment, poor conditions and racial pay, and INA inspiration.
With RIAF strikes too, the 'martial races' myth broke and the British saw that the armed forces, the last reliable instrument, were cracking.
46: Rajagopalachari proposed that ML1906 back Purna Swaraj and join a coalition at the Centre.
Jinnah wanted only Muslims to vote, a fully separate Pakistan (Two Nations, Two States) and all of it before the British left.
Bhulabhai Desai and Liaqat Ali Khan agreed on a VEC of Indians with 50% INC and 50% ML1906, and 20% of legislature seats for minorities. Gandhi knew of it.
After the QIM leaders were released, Wavell4347 held the Shimla Conference in June 1945 and proposed a VEC of Indians with 50% Hindus and 50% Muslims.
Wavell4347 declared failure because ML1906 could not be convinced, an implicit veto at the top. ML1906's prestige soared and it swept the seats reserved for Muslims, winning Bengal and Sindh.
Atlee became PM in July 1945, Japan surrendered, the INA trials united Indians, and the Naval Mutiny broke out on the day the Cabinet Mission arrived.
A weak centre for Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs, three sections A, B and C, and a Constituent Assembly of PLA members plus princely nominees.
INC declared NWFP and Assam would not join Groups B and C, and Nehru said only the Constituent Assembly was binding.
In February 1947 Atlee fixed 30 June 1948 for the British exit, with or without a constitution, and Paramountcy was not to pass to any successor.
INC accepted partition and dominion status in return for a small Pakistan, a strong centre and exit by 15 August 1947.
The Indian Independence Act of July 1947 gave legal form to the plan and ended Paramountcy over all 565 states. Patel and V.P.
47: Modern industry created workers in the second half of the 19th century. Early unions were welfare bodies (Lokhande 1890) and then the Madras Labour Union (1918). Their strikes had no wider politics.
Naoroji's 1886 rule kept class issues out of Congress to protect unity with zamindars and Indian industry.
Swadeshi strikes, the Tilak trial protest and the war-time price rise drew workers in. AITUC (1920) gave an all-India body; C.R.
CPI arrived via Tashkent 1920 and Kanpur 1925 (Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, Joshi). The Trade Union Act 1926 recognised unions while Meerut and the 1929 bills coerced them.
Colonial tariffs and credit starved Indian business, so FICCI (1927) tied itself to the INC.
Walangkar, Vaikom, Periyar's Self-Respect Movement and Guruvayur attacked untouchability. Ambedkar moved to water (Mahad 1927), burnt the Manusmriti and demanded separate electorates.
Gandhi's fast unto death ended with joint electorates and more reserved seats. INC won only half of reserved seats in 1937; Ambedkar's ILP and AISCF were squeezed.
Reformers spoke about women, not with them.
Prices halved 1929-33 but rent and debt did not; CDM politicised the peasantry and the left organised it.
INC ministries struck middle-path agrarian deals and used police on Bakasht (about 600 arrests).
Worli, Bakasht, Punnapra-Vayalar, Tebhaga and Telangana fought feudal extraction, some serving national integration and some outside the Gandhian frame.
